Lately, I have noticed a deeply concerning trend in technical recruitment, especially targeting senior systems, engine, and game developers working with C++, Rust, and various Game Engines.

Platforms are reaching out with high-paying, short-term offers for AI evaluation projects. The catch is always the same. Before a single interview is scheduled, and before any NDA or contract is signed, you are asked to submit your repository links, playable builds, and a 5-minute video walkthrough explaining your architectural choices, memory management, and engineering workflows.

Let's call this what it actually is. This isn't a traditional hiring funnel. It is mass data harvesting disguised as a job application.

The tech giants behind frontier AI models (like OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta) have a massive problem right now. They have already scraped the entire public internet and exhausted open-source platforms, but their models still struggle with high-level logic. Now, they are desperately trying to lay their hands on proprietary work and internal engineering reasoning.

When you record a video breaking down your code, you are giving away the holy grail of AI training, which is expert human feedback (RLHF). You are teaching a future model exactly how a senior engineer thinks, and you are doing it completely for free with zero guarantees of employment.

However, there is no such thing as free lunch. If these corporations want to train their models on our real-world engineering processes, they need to hire us as legitimate contractors and pay for every single repository and video session we provide. We cannot allow our years of expertise to be devalued just so a handful of AI companies can maximize their profit margins.

Personally, this pervasive data grabbing has forced me to completely alter my workflow to protect my intellectual property. Due to widespread unauthorized scraping and aggressive recruitment tactics, I actually had to remove my public repositories from GitHub and other open platforms to safeguard my IP.

On top of that, I stopped using cloud-based AI coding assistants because they treat every single line of user input as free training data. Instead, I now rely exclusively on offline, locally hosted models that I often have to fine-tune myself to meet the demands of advanced systems programming.

We need to protect our code and our engineering judgment. Your expertise is worth a premium, and it should never be given away under the pressure of a rushed application deadline. If a platform demands your IP upfront without a contract, just walk away.

Too expensive to compete with small teams. Too small to compete with the giants.
That's where most service firms are right now.

We've seen this before. In 2002 the Dallas Morning News had about 520,000 readers. Today around 61,000. The New York Times went the other way, from 1.1 million to more than 13 million subscribers. And Lenny Rachitsky, an ex-Airbnb product manager writing a newsletter on his own, has over a million.

When the internet made distribution free, newspapers didn't shrink evenly. A few giants got bigger, a lot of small one-person publications appeared, and the middle got squeezed.

I think the same is now happening to every service business that grows by hiring people. Agencies, consultancies, software houses, law firms.

When the work gets cheap, the market splits:
- On one side, a few very big players. Brand, big contracts, and money to put AI into everything.
- On the other side, a lot of very small teams. One to five people, AI doing most of the production, selling a result instead of hours.

...and in the middle, the 50–300 person firm selling people by the month. Stuck between the two.

You can already see it in law. Big firms just had a record year billing hours. At the same time, new AI startups sell a contract review for a fixed price of about £95. The top and the bottom are doing fine. The pressure is in the middle.

Under my last post about software houses dying, someone wrote a smart comment: when his seniors got faster, they didn't bill fewer hours, they started to own a bigger piece of the product. I think that's the way out of the middle. You become a small team that owns results, or you grow into a big one that owns a whole category.

Today I'm a company of one, and it's on purpose.

Newspapers had 10 years to see it coming. Most of them didn't. Service firms have maybe 2–3. So what will separate the ones that make it from the ones that are already too late?

Too expensive to compete with small teams. Too small to compete with the giants. That's where most service firms are right now.

In 2002 the Dallas Morning News had about 520,000 readers. Today around 61,000. The New York Times went the other way. From 1.1 million to more than 13 million subscribers. And Lenny Rachitsky, an ex-Airbnb product manager writing a newsletter on his own, has over a million. 

When the internet made distribution free, newspapers didn't die evenly. The middle died. A few giants got bigger, a lot of small one-person publications appeared, and everything in between got squeezed. As a follow-up to my last post about software houses, I think the same is now happening to every service business that grows by hiring people. 

Agencies, consultancies, software houses, law firms. When the work gets cheap, the market splits: 
- On one side, a few very big players. Brand, big contracts, and money to put AI into everything. 
- On the other side, a lot of very small teams. One to five people, AI doing most of the production, selling a result instead of hours. 

And in the middle, the 50–300 person firm selling people by the month. Too expensive to compete with the small ones. Too small to compete with the big ones. You can already see it in law. Big firms just had a record year billing hours. At the same time, new small AI startups sell a contract review for a fixed price of about £95. 

The top and the bottom are doing fine. The pressure is in the middle. 

Under my last post, someone wrote something smart: when his seniors got faster, they didn't bill fewer hours, they started to own a bigger piece of the product. I think that's the way out of the middle. You become a small team that owns results, or you grow into a big one that owns a whole category. 

Today Im a company of one, and its on purpose. 

Newspapers had 10 years to see it coming. Most of them didn't. Service firms have maybe 2–3. Which ones do you think will make it, and which are already too late?

Should the UK scrap non-competes, long notice periods and garden leave?

Several major UK AI / Tech leaders are calling for the government to take action on these "outdated practices" which they say hinder labour mobility and subsequently impact Britain's economy and productivity.

"In California, workers can start or join new companies overnight. If it is easier for companies to hire in California, they will hire in California."

"We therefore call on the Government to ban lengthy post-termination restrictions and restrict the use of extended notice periods and garden leave. These terms lower wages, reduce competition, and undermine the innovation that drives economic growth."

So far this letter has been signed by Tantum Collins at Inherent, Walter Goodwin at Fractile, Simon Kohl at Latent Labs, Chad Edwards at CuspAI, Victor Riparbelli at Synthesia, Mati Staniszewski at ElevenLabs, Jascha Achterberg at Callosum, Tim Rocktäschel at Recursive and a whole host of other leaders and founders from some of the most exciting companies in the UK AI & Tech ecosystem.

(I'll include a link to the full letter which you can add your name to in the comments)



3-month notice periods have always seemed crazy to me. They're almost never truly needed, and having that much more time to bring in a replacement means that companies tend to be more complacent and take longer to hire, leaving work in a period of limbo or lumping the work onto the plates of others. Give them a month and they tend to act with far more urgency, hire far faster and have less impact on product roadmaps and colleague workloads.

It also often leads to a somewhat inevitable degree of resentment / checking out on the leaver's part which can have real impact on those around them.

And I have certainly made UK hires for US firms who have struggled with getting their head around 3 month notice periods and reconsidered whether hiring here is the right choice (even though their own UK contracts included 3 month notice periods!)

Launched in 2015 (pic 1), sold in 2018 (pic 2), here’s how we did it…


Whenever I say I sold my business within 3 years the first questions I get are how and why?! So here are some thoughts…

How: 

 - LASER focus on core product. It’s easy to add more strings to your bow, but being the number one in something specific can be highly lucrative. 

- PROFITABLY built in from day one. While most competitors were focussed on variable percentage revenue based on media spend, we focused on fixed retainers ensuring guaranteed revenue every month.

 - AUTOMATE or die. AI wasn’t a thing when we were growing so we had to build automation tools to make the business more efficient and less labour intensive. Nowadays you have no excuses!

 - CONTRACTS are king! Ensuring client contracts were clear and concise when it came to generating additional work ensured we could charge rather than just becoming yes men and doing work for free, a trap many fall in to. 

 - TEAMWORK really makes the dream work. Hiring the right people and empowering them to make quick decisions without micro managing. 

Why:

I’ve had many question on why we sold so early, but the answer is very straight forward.

  - You can’t be greedy and you never know what lurks around the corner. We knew as a niche business that we had a few years of growth left but beyond that was a huge unknown. Knowing when to sell is an art-form in itself, but if there’s a life changing offer on the table, then IMO you should be seriously considering it. 

 - We were in a very fortunate position and were highly profitable from day one, so when you’re looking at multiples, time is irrelevant, so we looked at where we were, and where we needed to get to with an earn out and the numbers and timelines made sense. 

Happy building 💪🏻💪🏻

Technology hiring is changing.
Companies are no longer looking at contract hiring only when there is an immediate vacancy. Increasingly, businesses are using flexible talent models to prepare for upcoming projects, changing skill requirements and fluctuating workloads.
Some of the emerging trends we are seeing in contract hiring include:
• Skills first hiring instead of relying only on job titles and resumes
 • Ready to deploy talent for faster project mobilisation
 • Remote contract teams supporting projects across locations
 • Specialised talent pools for AI, Data, Cloud, Cybersecurity, Salesforce and ServiceNow
 • Flexible workforce models that can scale up or down with project demand
 • Stronger focus on technical assessment to validate actual capabilities
 • Bench strength becoming an important part of workforce readiness

The biggest shift is simple:
Businesses are increasingly planning for access to talent, not just headcount.
When the right skills are available at the right time, organisations can respond to opportunities and project requirements without waiting for lengthy hiring cycles.

Where is tomorrows talent coming from?

If AI takes on more of the work juniors learn from, how do they build the judgement we expect from senior hires?
For fund management firms and senior leaders across legal and compliance, that question is worth asking now.

In law practice, where many of the inhouse lawyers come from, early stage document review, research and first drafts serve two purposes; they get the work done, and they give junior lawyers experience. Reviewing a document, missing something and understanding a senior associates or partners correction are all part of learning.

As more of that work has becomes AI led, where is the opportunity to cut their teeth?
If the hierarchy in law practice was rejigged for AI to do first review and associates over see the AI, fairly well constructed but incorrect points, may get missed.  
If that review moves straight to senior lawyers, where does the junior gain the experience.

In fund management compliance, the challenge is similar, but there is no direct entry route like a training contract.
Compliance monitoring, routine business queries and process driven work can give junior compliance officers, exposure to how a fund operates, engagement with senior stakeholders and refined knowledge on FCA rules.
If firms automate more of those tasks and reduce entry-level hiring, the consequences could extend well beyond today’s team.

Less investment in that key development, across both role types would result in a much narrower pool of subject matter experts in the future.  Firms that invest in early stage talent now, could reap the benefits in years to come.  Small talent pools and lack of practical knowledge in private markets was a problem they faced not long ago, its probably not something we want to regress back to.

80% firm z listy Global 500. Tyle - według prognozy Gartnera z 15 września - do 2030 roku wpisze w umowę ze swoim CIO lub CAIO nową rolę: „Evidence Custodian". Osoba, która potrafi udowodnić, jak i dlaczego AI podjęła konkretną decyzję.

Czytam to jako koniec pewnej epoki: polityk AI pisanych na półkę. I początek czegoś, co każdy zarząd zna z własnego doświadczenia - za decyzję odpowiada się nie intencją, tylko udokumentowanym działaniem.

Ciekawy jest też drugi wątek tej samej prognozy: to ubezpieczyciele, nie regulatorzy, mają do 2030 roku kształtować governance AI - przez warunki polis od odpowiedzialności. Udokumentowane działanie przestaje być kwestią zgodności. Staje się kwestią wysokości składki.

Dla firm w Polsce i CEE to raczej szansa niż obowiązek. Jeśli agent AI już dziś wspiera decyzje kredytowe, rekrutacyjne czy cenowe, to firmy, które potrafią odtworzyć „dlaczego padła taka, a nie inna", będą miały przewagę - w rozmowie z klientem, audytorem i ubezpieczycielem.

Governance powoli przestaje być slajdem w prezentacji. Staje się linią w umowie.

Przez 20 lat pracy z zarządami widziałem wiele transformacji, w których odpowiedzialność za technologię była rozproszona tak skutecznie, że nie miał jej nikt. Teraz ktoś z imienia i nazwiska weźmie ją kontraktowo. Zaskakująco prosty pomysł - dziwne, że trzeba było AI, żeby na niego wpaść. 😉

[Eng]
80% of Global 500 companies. That's how many - according to Gartner's 15 September forecast - will by 2030 write a new role into their CIO's or CAIO's contract: "Evidence Custodian". The person able to prove how and why AI made a specific decision.

I read it as the end of an era: AI policies written for the shelf. And the start of something every board knows from experience - you answer for a decision not with intentions, but with documented action.

The second thread of the same forecast is just as interesting: by 2030, insurers - not regulators - are expected to shape AI governance, through liability policy terms. Documented action stops being a compliance matter. It becomes a matter of the premium.

For companies in Poland and CEE this is more an opportunity than an obligation. If an AI agent already supports credit, hiring or pricing decisions, the firms able to reconstruct "why this one and not another" will have the edge - with clients, auditors and insurers alike.

Governance is slowly ceasing to be a slide in a deck. It's becoming a line in a contract.

In 20 years of working with boards I've seen many transformations where accountability for technology was spread so effectively that nobody had it. Now someone, by name, will take it contractually. A surprisingly simple idea - strange it took AI to get us there. 😉

I think a lot of AI startups are going to die for a very boring reason.

They built something that can do 47 things.

Nobody urgently needed any of them.
There’s been a weird race to build “AI for businesses.”

AI that writes.
AI that researches.
AI that automates.
AI that helps teams “work smarter.”
Cool.

But who is actually desperate enough to pay for it?
The AI products I find most interesting aren't trying to be useful to everyone.
They're painfully specific.

AI for lawyers.
AI for accountants.
AI for sales teams.
AI for compliance.

AI for one very annoying workflow that currently costs someone 20 hours a week.
That's where the real opportunity is.
Because people don't really buy AI.

They buy outcomes.
A lawyer doesn't wake up thinking:
“I need some AI today.”
They think:
“I need to review 300 contracts without hiring another person.”
That's a much better business.

And I think this matters even more in Africa.
There are thousands of incredibly specific problems sitting inside African businesses that nobody has built properly for yet.

Tax.
Compliance.
Payroll.
Cross-border payments.
Import/export.
Licensing.
Healthcare administration.
The list is ridiculous.

You don't necessarily need another “AI platform for African businesses.”
Maybe you just need to find one extremely painful problem and become ridiculously good at solving it.

The interesting question isn't:
“Where can we add AI?”
It's:
“What problem is painful enough that people will pay us to make it disappear?”
That's where I'd start.

Remote jobs are not gone. You are just searching the wrong words.

I use Perplexity to uncover global remote roles that most standard filters never surface.

Many companies don’t write:
“work from anywhere”

Instead, they describe it with terms like:
• contract
• freelance
• global team
• work across time zones
• anywhere
• outside the US
• remote in selected countries

That tiny wording shift makes a big difference.

Here is the simple workflow:

1/ Search for hiring signals
In Perplexity, prompt:

“Find companies hiring for [your role] that may accept people from many countries. Look for words like contract, freelance, global team, work across time zones, anywhere, or outside the US. Skip jobs that clearly need US-only hiring. Show me the company, job link, country limits, job type, and why it may fit.”

Now you’re not just searching for “remote.”
You’re searching the language companies actually use.

2/ Check the company pages
Then ask:

“Check company career pages, founder posts, and hiring pages for this role. Find companies that look open to global remote workers, even if the job title does not say work from anywhere.”

This is how you catch roles that filters skip.

3/ Save the good ones
Drop the results into Notion or Google Sheets.

Track:
• company
• role
• link
• country limit
• time zone need
• job type
• notes

4/ Match your CV to that kind of job
Use ChatGPT or Claude.
Ask it to rewrite your strongest CV points to emphasize:
• working alone
• clear writing
• fast work
• working with people in different time zones
• real results

The best global remote jobs are often not inside the “remote” filter.
They’re sitting behind simple words.

AI helps you spot them faster.

Every AI assistant is good at something. The trick is giving it the right job.
Here's who we'd hire for what.

ChatGPT gets the all-rounder role. It covers the widest range of tasks, it's strong on complex coding, and its deep research mode builds detailed reports from multiple sources.

Claude gets the writing. It handles nuance well and reasons across long documents, which suits contracts, specifications and policy work.
Google Gemini gets the job if your business runs on Google Workspace. It works inside Docs and Gmail and includes built-in image and video generation.

Microsoft Copilot gets the job if you run on Windows and Microsoft 365. It sits inside Outlook, Teams, Word and Excel, the tools your team already opens every morning.

Notice something about the last two. They're chosen largely for where they live, not what they do.

That's often the real decision. The best assistant is usually the one that fits the systems your people already use, because that's the one they'll actually use.

Hiring the tool is the easy part. Knowing which processes to point it at, and which ones to leave alone, is where the value sits.

Most people assume Meta can just flip a switch, bundle Muse and their business agents, and instantly compete with Microsoft or AWS in the enterprise space.

I am not convinced it will be that simple.

Hiring MongoDB's former CEO is a smart move, but enterprise software is fundamentally different from consumer scale or open-source weight. It is not just about raw model performance or shipping developer tools like Muse Code and the Muse API. Enterprise adoption lives and dies on boring things: compliance, governance, multi-tenant security, legacy integrations, and predictable support contracts.

Meta has built an incredible tech stack, but their DNA is consumer-first advertising and developer open-source goodwill. Selling closed, mission-critical infrastructure to risk-averse IT departments requires a completely different operational playbook.

Great models alone do not win the enterprise. The real test is whether Meta can build the enterprise trust layer before existing incumbents close the capability gap.
